VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01642

Jildaki suggests both the beginning of these stages and their anticipated final fulfillment in the very name he gives the “Child of Renewal”—the child he, the alchemist, already is. He calls him ‘Abd al-Karim, the servant of the Noble (Stone). At the first dawning of his new birth, he is indeed the servant of the Noble Stone, which he must serve until the triumphant end, when he takes on the form of the filius regius, the royal son invested with divine power. Here is the whole Aenigma regis, the riddle of the king: the sacred marriage of heaven and earth, to be consummated in novissimo die hujus artis, on the Last Day that brings the Work to completion.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01643

Expressed in the language of mystical alchemy, Suhrawardi’s theme of Hermes and Perfect Nature thus carries to their furthest reach the meanings we have already drawn from the symbolism of the archangel Gabriel’s “two wings.” In this Hermetic tradition we glimpse in advance the union of Lover and Beloved, the longing for which fills all Persian poetry. And if Suhrawardi’s psalm addresses Perfect Nature as the One-Who-Gives-Birth-and-Is-Born, it is because Perfect Nature gives birth to herself in Hermes precisely as Hermes (or the priest in Zosimos’s dream) is brought to birth in himself. Likewise, the Beloved, though grammatically the one who receives love, is at the same time the one who brings love into being within the Lover, giving birth to herself there as Beloved precisely by giving birth to him as Lover.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01644

We might say that the alchemical expression of Perfect Nature’s secret makes one thing clearer than any other: for the Gnostic in this world there are two “guardian angels,” the “root” and the “branch.” There is the angel who is his parens, his heavenly father or mother before he comes into this world; and there is the angel who is his child—his own future self, born into his Perfect Nature for a life beyond this world. When he has become this “Child” entirely (when the hoopoe has become the Simurgh), the self that belonged “to this world” has been brought home “to its own world.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01645

Only the pair of “two angels” remains. This is what justifies Suhrawardi’s invocation of Perfect Nature as both the one who gives birth and the one who is born. It is also why Latin alchemy was so fond of the symbol of the Virgin Mother. Here, once again, we may quote a couplet by Angelus Silesius: “If God’s Spirit touches you with its being, the Child of Eternity is born in you.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01646

e) Manichaean Gnosis and Zoroastrianism. In the preceding pages we have assembled the themes of the image and the mirror as variations on the theme of the angel. Passing through Mithraic material and alchemy, we have returned to Perfect Nature—the supreme expression of the personal angel in Suhrawardi’s spiritual philosophy. All this now comes to a head in the search for analogies, if not direct precedents, within the spirituality of ancient Persia, which the Shaykh al-Ishraq sought to revive.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01647

Manichaean gnosis, in fact, knows of a luminous primordial Nature, a divine being whom one of the fragments recovered at Turfan praises as “our father and our mother, our magnificence, our Self of Splendor”—that is, our Nature of Light, our primordial Self. “Hail to you, with whom our soul has been identical from the first beginning” .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01648

We are brought back to the questions Suhrawardi’s writings had led us to ask (above, p. 295). Who is the personal Angel? What is the relation between Perfect Nature as personal Angel and the Angel encountered on Sinai, since both are called the mystic’s “father”? We saw how the vision itself, and the symbol in which it finds expression, dissolved the apparent dilemma: is it one angel or the other? That insight opens the path we must now follow.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01649

Scholars have devoted particular attention to the nature and powers of the being of light known in Manichaeism as “Great Vahman,” or in Parthian as “Great Manuhmed” or “Manvahmed.” The name derives from the Avestan Vohu Manah (Persian Bahman). As we recalled earlier (p. 112), Zoroastrianism uses this name for the first of the “Holy Immortals” (Amahraspands), the archangels. Broadly, it means Good Spirit, Luminous Thought, or Nous of Light—the luminous spiritual Intellect. We have also seen it occupying the highest rank in Suhrawardi’s angelology.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01650
But what is the relation between this Nous of Light and the individual “Manvahmeds” or “Vahmanans”?
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01651

One may see in “Great Manvahmed” the Perfect Man, identifying it with the “Column of Glory,” the “Column of Light” formed by the ascending procession of all souls freed from Darkness and returning to the kingdom of Light. From this, one might conclude that all the Vahmanans together constitute Great Vahman or Great Manvahmed.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01652

But that reduces Great Manvahmed to a merely collective being and, in doing so, abolishes the very relationship and function essential to it: the relationship between the saving Angel and the individual soul it saves. Their unity as two does not disappear when the salvation brought by the savior restores it to its original state. The collective interpretation replaces these twofold unities with single units. It would then have to be the “Self of Splendor” itself that was held captive by Darkness.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01653

Yet it is precisely this “Self of Splendor” that speaks to the captive as the captive’s Angel. The situation is thus like that of Perfect Nature as the Gnostic’s angel. Perfect Nature gives an individual form to the relation between the Angel and each of the beings that together make up the whole of which the Angel is the guardian. That whole consists of all these twofold unities, each made up of a Gnostic and his Perfect Nature.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01654
The vocabulary used by the neo-Manichaeism of the Cathars points us toward the same solution. It also helps us preserve the distinct themes and the parallel relationships between these terms.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01655

First there is the human soul, earthly and captive: Anima. Then there is its holy or angelic spirit (Spiritus sanctus, angelicus, or paraclitus). Each elect soul has its own. This is the “guardian angel” in the Gnostic sense: the Heavenly Double, the Spirit that has “remained in heaven” and acts as protector.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01656

Finally there is the Spiritus principalis, corresponding to the saving Primordial Man or the Nous of Light, invoked through the names of the three persons of the Trinity. The cosmic Spirit or Nous stands in relation to the totality of souls as each individual Nous, Spirit, or angel stands in relation to its own soul. We are dealing, then, with a parallel between two pairs of terms, not simply with a relation between two terms .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01657

This means that Great Vahman, the cosmic Nous, has a distinct existence of its own, alongside the holy Spirits or Heavenly Doubles, each of which stands to its individual soul as Great Vahman stands to the totality of souls. It is not Great Vahman as such, but each of these holy Spirits, that is the Heavenly Double of a particular soul. Suhrawardi’s symbolism of the two wings presents the same situation. The Angel exists as a spiritual being in its own right, while its two wings are its “members.” They symbolize the multitude of pairs that together form the order of beings over which it presides as Angel or lord (rabb), each pair consisting of a soul and its Nous.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01658

We must also remember that, according to the Iranian way of counting, a whole has a unity of its own in addition to the units that compose it; it is not simply their sum. Great Vahman must therefore have a reality distinct from its parts and from their total .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01659

For their part, the philosophers of Illumination (Ishrâqîyûn) repeatedly insisted that the universality of each angel-archetype is not the universality of a logical concept. It is the metaphysical universality of an essence, subject neither to the conditions of the logical universal—which is poorest in content—nor to the conditions under which such a universal is realized in singularibus, in individual things belonging to the world of the senses. This essence is fully and unconditionally what it is. That is what they perceive in the “person” of the archetypal Angel, the lord of a species whose existence is its “theurgy,” its divine work, and whose salvation the Angel brings about.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01660

The theme of the Heavenly Double receives its fullest force in the mystery of salvation. In Manichaeism, its development concerns Mani himself before anyone else . When Mani is twenty-four, the Angel appears to him as his “double” or “twin” and announces that the time has come for him to reveal himself and summon people to his teaching: “Greetings to you, O Mani, from me and from the Lord who has sent me to you ...” Some of Mani’s words as he lay dying also refer to this Heavenly Double: “I contemplated my Double with my eyes of light.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01661

Yet a psalm celebrating the soul’s departure from earthly existence also speaks of “your Double who never failed.” Every soul, then, truly has its Double. Mani’s Heavenly Double may be Christ in the Western Manichaean tradition, or the Virgin of Light in the Eastern tradition; but each soul likewise has its own Double, its partner in a sacred pair, its Nous: the Heavenly Double who guides it to the kingdom of Light when it dies to the Earth.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01662
It is therefore the individual Nous that appears to its soul, its earthly child, in order to strengthen, guide, and save it. It is the Nous of this particular soul.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01663

Yet, as a “member” of the cosmic Nous, it accomplishes the whole salvation of that soul, just as cosmic salvation is the work of the great Nous as a whole. The individual Nous is a “member” of the great Nous in the same way that the individual soul is a member of its own Nous. This pattern, repeated on two levels, clarifies the familiar theological theme of the “members.” Its gradation is beautifully expressed in a Parthian hymn: “Come, soul, do not be afraid. I am your Manvahmed, your pledge and your seal, and you are my body, a robe I have put on to frighten the powers. And I am your light, the original radiance, Great Manvahmed, the Perfect Pledge” .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01664

Thus an individual Nous can also present itself, to a particular soul, as Great Manvahmed. This possibility points to a very precise kind of relationship—exactly the one taught by Valentinian Gnostic angelology. There the Angels of Christ are acknowledged to be Christ himself, in the sense that each Angel, guided or sent by Christ, is Christ himself in relation to a particular individual existence .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01665

We may recall that, in the “Tale of Exile,” the Angel on Sinai reveals to the Elect that above him, on a higher Sinai, stands another Angel. His relation to that higher Angel is the same as the Elect’s relation to him: the higher Angel “contains” him just as he “contains” the Elect. At every level, the two intelligible dimensions are repeated from Angel to Angel: from the “right wing” proceeds a new Intelligence, and from the “left wing” the soul of that Intelligence. And so it continues, from one mystical Sinai to the next. The drama that befalls the Tenth Angel, the Angel of humanity, is symbolized by the darkening of his “left wing”—the souls held captive in this world.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01666

At this level, already very far removed from the Principle, the procession of being no longer has the power to bring forth one Intelligence and one Soul. Instead, as we have said, it breaks into a multitude of pairs, and the two members of each pair are separated. On one side stands the Self of Light, or Perfect Nature; on the other, cut off from it, the “exiled” self. This is the Gnostic pattern itself. Salvation means reuniting the two, freeing the exiled self from its darkness. The reunion therefore has two forms at once: an individual reunion within each pair, and a collective reunion embracing all these pairs with their respective Nous.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01667

But the collective depends on the individual; the salvation of the whole can take place only through the salvation of each of its “members.” The catastrophe and its resolution, recurring themes in Suhrawardi’s tales, are thus rooted in the very Iranian gnosis that the Shaykh al-Ishraq sought to bring back to life.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01668

We have already had occasion to recall what the Fravartis (Persian Foruhar) are in Zoroastrianism. They are heavenly beings, archetypes of every creature belonging to Ohrmazd’s world of light; they exist in the subtle spiritual world before the manifested world comes into being. The relation between the Fravarti and the soul (urvân, ravân) would thus be comparable to that between the Heavenly Double and the earthly self, or between Perfect Nature and the exiled self.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01669

But here we must take account of a dramatic episode at the heart of Zoroastrian cosmology and its teaching on the soul’s final destiny. The Fravartis—“those who have chosen”—accepted the task of descending to Earth themselves. They voluntarily left the world of light to help Ohrmazd in the struggle they would wage together against the opposing power of Ahriman. For this reason, the final reunion is not simply a reunion of the soul with its Fravarti; it is a reunion of the Fravarti-soul with its Heavenly Double, the Daena . Scholars have debated at length how the word Daena can mean both “religion” and a person’s “transcendent” or “heavenly self,” and how it can carry both a collective and an individual meaning.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01670

But here we can recognize just the sort of false dilemma that Suhrawardi has helped us overcome in the preceding pages. As the “religion” of Ohrmazd, the “Lord Wisdom,” Daena is indeed what the Fravarti chose before its earthly existence. It is therefore entirely capable of representing the preexistent, heavenly, or transcendent Self of a being of light. (Shiite gnosis, too, will teach that a being’s religion, Dîn, is that being’s imperishable Face.) This is the living presence at the heart of the believer, inspiring some of the most beautiful surviving texts of Zoroastrian theology, which describe the encounter with the Angel Daena after death .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01671

On the third day after death—after the exitus—the Elect, approaching the Chinvat Bridge, sees a dazzling Form coming toward him: a young woman more beautiful than any beauty he has seen on Earth. Wonderstruck, he asks, “Who are you?” She replies: “I am your Daena ... (your religion and your own self), the one whom your thoughts, your words, and your deeds have made. I was loved; you made me more loved. I was beautiful; you made me more beautiful still.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01672

Let us remember that Hermes, too, asks the mysterious Form of Light who reveals the higher knowledge to him: “Who are you?” The answer comes: “I am your Perfect Nature.” As his psalm to her attests, Suhrawardi knows that his Perfect Nature exists before him, for it is she who brings him to birth in the spiritual world.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01673

But he also knows that, at the same time, he brings her to birth. Likewise Daena already existed, since the believer chose her before entering this world; yet she is also the one whom his thoughts, words, and deeds have made. They grow together, just as the light-colored robe does in the “Hymn of the Pearl” from the Acts of Thomas. If all these are variations on the same encounter, we may also say that meeting Daena is no different from meeting the Image or “icon” spoken of in the “Gospel according to Thomas,” Mandaean gnosis, and, above all, the Manichaean account of the soul’s destiny after death.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01674

Indeed, the Manichaean vision brings the details of the scene into even sharper focus. Two passages from Mani’s Kephalaia deserve quotation. One describes the Form of Light revealed to each of the Elect as they leave their bodies, accompanied by three great and splendid Angels. The first brings the prize of victory, the second the robe of light, and the third the diadem of light .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01675

Another passage describes “the moment when they depart this world, when the Form of Light comes to meet them and separates them from Darkness, leading them to the Light ... The Form of Light calms the man with a kiss and with peace, freeing him from fear of the demons that destroy his body. By her appearance and her image (icon, eikôn), the heart of the Elect who leaves his body is set at rest. Then the Angel who holds the prize of victory stretches out his right hand and receives him with a kiss and with love. Then this soul pays homage to the one who saves it, who is this Form of Light” .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01676

This Form of Light, then, is indeed the Angel who comes to meet the soul after death. It is also the Angel described in Ibn al-Nadim’s Arabic Fihrist as a divinity of light, sent to the soul by the Primordial Anthropos, or First Man, in the form of the “wise guide.” Three other beings of light accompany this figure, along with “the maiden who resembles the soul.” All come to help the soul resist the demons that would attack it. Who, then, is the “wise guide”? That title is especially striking because its Arabic form (al-Hakîm al-Hâdî) corresponds word for word to the title at the beginning of the “Tale of the Western Exile.” There, too, it designated the “wise guide” who would finally appear as the Angel on Sinai.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01677

A Manichaean treatise in Sogdian gives us an answer to the question raised by the Fihrist. Where the preceding text spoke of one Form of Light, the Fihrist divides it into two figures: the wise guide and the one who resembles the soul. The Sogdian text describes the Angels descending to meet the soul of the Elect, to reassure and protect it. “Do not be afraid, righteous soul ... Go forward ... ascend to the paradise of Light, receive Joy.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01678

And then: “His own Action, a marvelous and divine princess, a young woman, will come to meet him, immortal, her head adorned with flowers ... She herself will set him on the road to the paradise of Light.” Other Coptic texts also describe the maiden who becomes the soul’s guide. The Sogdian fragment just quoted therefore shows more clearly than any other—as Henning wrote—that “the Manichaeans shared the Zoroastrian conception of a man’s Daena, who meets him after death in the form of a young woman” .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01679

It is explicitly this maiden who is called the guide, the one who “sets the Elect on the road.” At the same time, because she is the soul’s own Action, she truly resembles the soul, just as the soul resembles her. Guide and image are therefore joined in the very “person” of the Angel Daena. She is indeed the Double of Light whose dialogue with her earthly soul we heard earlier. We have already said that this sacred pairing places a mutual responsibility upon its two members. Daena will answer for the man after death to the degree that he has answered for Daena during his earthly life.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01680

Once again, neither metaphor nor allegory is at work here. If Daena is the Action of the earthly man, it is because that Action will have taken form in his likeness. The mystery of the sacred union after death—a union whose preparation or anticipation requires a new birth—is the mystery of the One-Who-Gives-Birth-and-Is-Born, where acting and receiving action pass into one another. Daena’s birth through and within the human soul, as that soul’s own Action, is at the same time the birth of the soul in and through the Angel Daena who is acting within it.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01681
This is precisely the meaning already suggested to us both by the symbolism of the Angel’s “two wings” and by the psalm Suhrawardi addresses to his Perfect Nature.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01682

We recalled earlier that the longing for this unifying reunion runs throughout Persian mysticism. It will reach one of its high points in Ruzbihan’s mysticism of love (see Book III). Each time, this reunion marks or announces the lover’s new birth. We should not accuse the images used by our mystics of logical contradictions that arise only at the level of concepts formed by the understanding. Beyond logical concepts are realities that can be expressed only in images.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01683

The relation between two beings joined as a pair—a syzygy—can be experienced and expressed through the image of marriage, the relation of lover and beloved; it can also be expressed through the image of parenthood, the relation of father and son. Each image expresses the same process of new birth, in which the roles of the two partners become reciprocal. The figures of Perfect Nature and the Angel on Sinai, of the Form of Light and the Angel Daena, overlap and take one another’s place.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01684

What remains is the idea of a sacred union to be fulfilled at the end of time, in novissimo die: the mystery of a new birth in which a being is brought forth in the image of its Heavenly Double, an image that the Double itself actively brings into reality within that being. It is the idea of a mystical coming-into-likeness and a shared responsibility that together announce the dawn of resurrection. These themes recur wherever the splitting apart of a primordial heavenly-earthly pair expresses the mystery of the Origin.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01685

Restoring the pair’s unity-in-twoness, its dualitude, then becomes the measure of an inner ethic, whose fulfillment will be precisely the final encounter and mutual recognition of a human being and his Angel. This is the event that dominates the horizon of Iranian teaching about the world to come and of Gnostic spirituality: in Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism, no less than in Christian gnosis and the philosophy of Illumination. “May you reveal yourself to me at the supreme epiphany,” Suhrawardi prayed in his psalm.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01686

In the end, all our inquiries into the Heavenly Double, the Angel, converge upon a sophiology: a spiritual understanding of divine Wisdom, Sophia, as a living figure. Elsewhere we have shown how, and in what respect, Daena and Sophia can be identified with one another . The vision of Perfect Nature granted to Hermes is also, in one respect, a vision of Sophia herself. As we saw earlier, Hermes teaches that Perfect Nature is the one who brings Wisdom down to Earth. She is the “philosopher’s angel,” the one who governs and guides him: the “wise guide.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01687

Our inquiries thus open onto a whole tradition of thought about Sophia, embracing Jacob Boehme and his school, especially Gottfried Arnold, and many others down to Vladimir Solovyov. This is not the place to pursue it; another book will be needed. That book would also have to gather the visible symbols perceived or formed in visionary meditation: a whole family of images able to express the restored dualitude brought about when the member cast into “Western exile” is transformed and transferred to the “generation beyond death.” We defined this dualitude earlier as unity of essence without confusion of persons.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01688

Suhrawardi’s symbolism of the Angel’s “two wings” has precisely this power to make us see. The Angel of human nature in its wholeness becomes visible only when Nous and Psyche, Perfect Nature and soul, earthly human being and the Angel Sophia-Daena, are reunited. In the same way, the reality of “heavenly” love is visible only in and for the unity of lover and beloved—a unity that is dualitude, not fusion, for it takes two to know the joy of being one.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01689

The echoes of this theme sound on in endless arpeggios. We cannot follow them here. But Swedenborg’s name must not be passed over in silence. The teachings of that great Swedish visionary and spiritual philosopher, and their influence on a whole family of minds, form the Western panel of the diptych whose Eastern panel we have just examined. A few lines must suffice as a brief reminder.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01690
f) Swedenborgian Parallels. In one of his Memorabilia, Swedenborg tells how, during a vision, he saw a chariot approaching from the far reaches of heaven. On it stood a magnificent Angel.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01691

But as the chariot drew closer, he realized that what had appeared from a distance to be a single Angel was in fact two angelic beings: a pair of heavenly lovers . Of course, the vision reveals its full meaning only when seen in the context of Swedenborg’s angelology as a whole and his teaching on heavenly love. Unfortunately, we cannot explore those teachings here.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01692

We shall remain within Swedenborg’s sphere of influence by considering another case: Balzac. We know how deeply Balzac was affected by his reading of Swedenborg and L.-C. de Saint-Martin. In November 1833, Balzac visited the sculptor Théophile Bra (1797–1863) , who was himself influenced by Swedenborg’s teachings and who created in stone one of the noblest and most solemn images of the “guardian angel.” During the visit, Balzac stood in Bra’s studio contemplating a sculptural group: the Virgin holding the Child, adored by two angels.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01693

The figures were extraordinarily beautiful. As Balzac continued looking, the image of the two angels took possession of his inner world of imagination. They became the image of two natures in one being—a being approaching its final transformation, who breaks open its outer covering and reveals to a man and a woman that it was this being whom they had loved when they loved the love that united them.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01694

Thus arose the idea for what would become Balzac’s mystical masterpiece: Seraphitus–Seraphita, one and the same angel, yet a double being, masculine and feminine, born from the union of lover and beloved. By freeing in each person “the angelic creature imprisoned within the flesh,” this angel embodies the dualitude of their love. The book ultimately appeared under the title Seraphita, and throughout it a tribute to Swedenborg and his teachings continues to resonate.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01695

These variations in the visible representation of the angel correspond, in their own way, to variations on the theme of the Gnostic’s encounter with the Angel. Much remains to be explored beyond what we have been able to suggest here.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01696

But we can now sum up what these texts have taught us about the nature of the human being and the meaning of human existence. On both sides, what emerges is the Gnostic experience of self-knowledge, which discovers the self as an alter ego, an “angel”—not, certainly, in the darkness of the unconscious, but in the “superlight” of a consciousness beyond ordinary consciousness.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01697

In that very experience the Gnostic knows he has been freed from exile, that is, from solitude. His full being is a dualitude: his ego is released from the isolation of mere egohood because, together with the heavenly alter ego of which he is the earthly counterpart, it forms a complete whole, a pleroma. This fullness is strong enough to overcome the opposing powers, whether they are called demonic or are the collective and social forces of “the city whose inhabitants are oppressors” (4:77).
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01698

The ultimate meaning of this restored dualitude appears in the vision of the soul’s destiny after death, shared by the different forms of gnosis we have considered. The Image each person brings to birth in this world, the ecstatic vision each gives form to here, determines what death will be for that person. What each has willed and anticipated in this life is precisely what each will see in the supreme vision and revelation on crossing the threshold. No one can hope, in the other world, to receive a vision that he has refused or desecrated, surrendering it to Darkness, in this one. The world of the Angel cannot answer for a human being who has refused to answer for it.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01699

Daena-Sophia will then be nothing but the extinguished heavenly past of the person who has disowned her. The terrifying vision that Zoroastrian texts describe as appearing to the demonic man—his own Action—has become a grotesque distortion of Daena. What he sees is his own self, handed over by its own denial to the nothingness of its solitude. That denial cuts it off from its Heavenly Double and leaves it marked by the mutilation of an infernal “unpairedness,” although its true nature was one of “pairedness” and heavenly dualitude. Such, it seems to us, is the meaning of a conception of the human being whose distant origins lie in the very sources of Iranian spirituality.

5. The Secret of the “Personal City”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01700

The preceding discussion has brought out several fundamental themes: the mirror, the image, and the idea of the human soul’s fullness, or pleroma, as a lesser Logos. The “Tale of Exile” and the “Treatise on the Rustling of Gabriel’s Wings” tell the “story” of this lesser Logos. It is the “story” of the Gnostic, whose different aspects we have just traced.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01701

But there is more. If the Gnostic descends into this world and is taken captive in the city of which it is said, “Our Lord! Bring us out of this city whose inhabitants are oppressors” (4:77), the Gnostic’s own person is also, in a corresponding vision of the imagination, represented as a city. The “city of the oppressors” is the world of illusion in which the lesser Logos presently dwells.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01702

But this lesser Logos is itself a city, one of those of which “God Most High has said: Of those cities We tell you their misfortune; some still stand, while others have been laid waste” (7:99 and 11:102). It is the “temple,” or dwelling place, of the lesser Logos that has been laid waste.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01703

But all the Logoi, all the Words of God, greater and lesser, “still stand”: they are the cities that endure, because they exist beyond time and the space of the senses . The Gnostic’s “story,” then, is the story of the personal city that endures, while the “city of the oppressors” is at last destroyed.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01704

This explains the importance of the theme not only for Suhrawardi—it shapes the vision of his “Treatise of the High Towers” (Risâlat al-abrâj)—but also for the whole body of metaphysical imagery surrounding the “Tale of Exile.” We would miss something essential if we ended without examining this imaginative vision of the Personal City.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01705

For that reason, it seems important to summarize a short treatise especially representative of Indo-Persian mystical literature. Although it is not Suhrawardi’s own work, it belongs closely to the cycle of his tales.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01706

Indeed, the treatise not only develops, in its own way, the recurring theme of “Western Exile”; several of its pages simply incorporate a chapter found in two of Suhrawardi’s narratives: the “Treatise of the High Towers” and the tale entitled “The Lovers’ Companion” (Mu’nis al-‘oshshâq). Taken as a whole, this Indo-Persian treatise is a perfect expression of the themes that shape the Gnostic’s spiritual adventure. In especially striking symbols, it recounts the Gnostic’s “story” as a search for himself, culminating in the encounter with his alter ego.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01707
By way of introduction to this little spiritual romance, let us say that it combines two themes: the mirror and the labyrinth. Neither word, it is true, occurs explicitly in the text.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01708

But what they signify is unmistakably present, and that is what matters. The feeling that the earthly world is a tomb in which beings from higher worlds lie buried is a constant feature of the Gnostic experience of this world. We find it expressed even in Shaykhi gnosis, in the writings of Sarkar Agha (see Book VI). Here, however, the image of the tomb becomes more complex and expansive: it becomes a labyrinth. Human existence now has a particular meaning. A being from the higher world is sent into this tomb so that it may learn to find the way out, as one finds the way out of a labyrinth (compare the “Tale of Exile,” stanza 37). The escape comes only after reaching the labyrinth’s heart, where the “Spring of Life” is found.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01709

But this departure can succeed only if we understand how the eternal Forms of the Malakût, the spiritual kingdom, are present in this perishable world. They do not become physically part of it. They are not inherent in it as blackness is inherent in a black object. They enter it as forms and images “enter” a mirror.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01710

Thus, to understand what we behold in this world, and where we behold it, is to understand what happens when we look into a mirror. It is within the whole human adventure, experienced as an “initiation,” that the hidden meaning of the tomb as labyrinth comes together with the phenomenon of the mirror. Their union is so essential that we find the mirror at the very “initiatory center” of the meaning of life, when life itself is portrayed as a labyrinth of bewildering turns and unforeseen events.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01711

We can best grasp the connection between the mirror and the labyrinth by turning to one of Leonardo da Vinci’s ingenious creations, wonderfully described by Marcel Brion . In the ancient myth, Theseus confronted the Minotaur at the heart of the labyrinth: the monstrous double of the human being, the man-bull. After killing it, Theseus emerged from the labyrinth as the spiritual hero of a purified humanity. In the central chamber of the labyrinth, an initiate into the mystery religions would meet the high priest, who explained the symbolic meaning of the ordeals and figures encountered along the way; the initiate emerged a new person.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01712

In certain Christian churches, a labyrinth marked out in the pavement—called the league of Jerusalem—allowed those unable to undertake an actual pilgrimage to make the sacred journey in soul and imagination. They followed its winding paths as a rite, facing dangers represented by symbolic monsters. Perhaps they reached the goal more directly in this way, since the final destination was not so much earthly Jerusalem as heavenly Jerusalem. And now Leonardo designs his own labyrinth. After an interminable journey along twisting paths, the initiate enters the central sanctuary for the supreme revelation. Here, however, the sanctuary is “an eight-sided room of mirrors that multiplies to infinity the image of the person standing at its center” .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01713

This central sanctuary is not the place where the monstrous Minotaur must be fought. Nor is it the place of divine contemplation sought by the medieval pilgrim in heavenly Jerusalem. It is the place where one contemplates oneself.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01714

But how far should we insist on the difference between contemplating oneself and contemplating the divine? To set them against each other is to miss the true meaning of this “self.” We would then risk misunderstanding the initiation offered by the “room of mirrors.” We avoid that danger if, with the spiritual writers we have been studying, we find in the vision of the mirror an answer to the question that governs the entire theory of knowledge: the question of how the forms of knowledge and consciousness come into being. Who is the “Giver of Forms,” the Dator formarum? To know the giver is to cease being enslaved by what is given. For to know the giver is to put into practice the fundamental maxim so often recalled in this book: “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01715

How, then, is the “self” known by one who knows himself connected with the “Giver of Forms”? The title “Giver of Forms” is bestowed in both the Latin metaphysical tradition (Dator formarum) and the Arabic (Wâhib al-Sowar) upon the spiritual being philosophers call the Active Intellect. Suhrawardi has already enabled us to recognize this being as the Angel on Sinai, who appears at the end of his “Tale of Exile.” Once again we find ourselves at the heart of questions explored at length in the preceding pages.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01716

We can already sense that the little Indo-Persian spiritual romance, which reveals something of the secret of the “Personal City,” will describe—with its own characters and scenery—the very journey whose stages are recounted in the “Tale of the Western Exile.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01717

The text survives in Arabic and Persian and claims to be translated from Sanskrit. The compilation can be no later than the fourteenth century, but it includes elements already found in Suhrawardi in the twelfth century .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01718

It may be an originally Iranian text that returned to Iran after migrating to India. Whatever its history, the work as a whole is a characteristic example of Sufism shaped by Indian influences. Its supposed narrator is a sage of India, who presents his spiritual autobiography in a symbolic form that closely corresponds both to Suhrawardi’s “Tale of the Western Exile” and to the adventures of the hero of the “Hymn of the Pearl,” the young Parthian prince in the Gnostic Acts of Thomas. We have already pointed out the parallels between those two journeys.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01719

The whole treatise takes the form of a narrative recounting the stages and adventures of initiation into the hidden meaning of the saying we have just recalled: “Whoever has known himself has known his God.” Between these two acts of knowing lies the whole drama of origin and return (mabda’ and ma‘âd). Its resolution reveals why the spiritual Forms “descend” into the “labyrinth.” For when they reach its heart, they discover, in the dazzling vision of a mirror, the answer to the question: Who am I?
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01720
The sage tells the story of his quest as follows: “Once I lived in my own country, the home of my parents and ancestors.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01721

“But one day the lord of the land summoned me and said: ‘It is fitting that you should not settle in the lofty dwellings of my kingdom until you have traveled to the land made fruitful by us, which lies at the farthest border of my realm. Do not forget our covenant of fidelity; for then you will find me there, in that distant land.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01722

“Ask my minister, who sits at my Threshold, to describe it to you. No one enters by that Threshold unless he knows him, and no one leaves except by my permission.’ When I reached the Threshold (bâb), I found him there. I greeted him, and he returned my greeting. ‘My lord and sovereign,’ I said, ‘has ordered me to journey to the land made fruitful by us.’ ‘To make this journey and reach its end,’ he said, ‘you will have to overcome obstacles and steep passages. And the return journey to us will be harder still.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01723

“I fear that distance and hardship will eventually cause you to forget our covenant.’ ‘Nevertheless, I must go,’ I said. ‘Describe that country to me. Describe the road that leads there.’” After warning him that the fatal act of forgetting would condemn the traveler to wander through ages upon ages, the “minister” gives the descriptions he has requested, then repeats his warning: “Do not forget our covenant. If you remember it, you will find us there—both me and my sovereign.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01724

What the “minister” describes are all the stages and adventures of the soul’s journey as it “descends” into this world. The pattern is common to the various forms of gnosis. The regions of the cosmos, the Spheres and the Elements, appear here as a cosmic labyrinth, through which the heavenly being—the pilgrim in this story—passes until it enters the narrow passages of the microcosm. This microcosm itself takes the form of a city, with a labyrinth of its own.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01725

The outer senses and inner faculties are portrayed as characters, each bearing the symbolic attributes of its function. They occupy the “junctions” of the labyrinth, which is nothing other than the pilgrim’s “Personal City.” Here we find, literally, the symbolic descriptions given by Suhrawardi in two of his mystical treatises, as we noted at the outset. Within the labyrinth of the Personal City, these figures play the same role as the symbolic characters encountered by pilgrims following the labyrinth marked out on church pavements.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01726

Turning this way and that, our pilgrim lingers and eventually forgets both his promises and the very reasons he came (the young Parthian prince of the “Hymn of the Pearl” suffers the same fate in Egypt).
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01727

Yet at last he reaches the heart of the city. There, at the heart of the labyrinth, the extraordinary encounter takes place: the mirror awakens the pilgrim to awareness of himself. He sees a shaykh, the master of the city, seated on a royal throne. “I greeted him,” the pilgrim relates, “and he returned my greeting. I spoke to him, and he spoke to me. Whatever I did, he did. Whatever I said, he said. I looked at him closely, and behold: he was myself; the shaykh was my reflected image (‘aksî). At once I awoke and remembered all the promises.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01728

“And while I was still dazzled by this discovery, I met the minister of my sovereign, the one who had instructed me. He took my hand and said: ‘Immerse yourself in this Water, for it is the Water of Life.’ When I had immersed myself, I understood the symbols and riddles of his person. He said: ‘Welcome! You are now one of us (anta minnâ)’ . And he announced my return to my country of origin.” This passage accords perfectly with what we read at the end of the “Tale of the Western Exile.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01729

Of course, with the help of parallel narratives—especially Suhrawardi’s—it would not be difficult to suggest several interpretations of the characters in this drama. The “sovereign” may be the Lord God. His “minister” would then be the Active Intellect, traditionally called the Dator formarum, the Giver of Forms, by philosophers, and identified by Suhrawardi’s “Eastern” spiritual philosophers, the Ishrâqîyûn, with the Holy Spirit and Angel of humanity. This Angel is at once the angel of Knowledge and the angel of Revelation, the Angel on Sinai in the “Tale of Exile.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01730

The shaykh at the city’s heart would then be Perfect Nature, the pilgrim’s heavenly alter ego. Or, still in terms of Suhrawardi’s philosophy, the three characters could stand respectively for the Angel-Intelligence that is the Dator formarum; Perfect Nature, the Gnostic’s personal angel; and the soul-self that has “descended” into this world. Suhrawardi calls this last, borrowing a term from the old Iranian chivalric tradition, the espahbad light, corresponding in a certain sense to the Stoic hêgemonikon, the soul’s governing faculty. A Shiite mystic, on the other hand, might see in the sovereign and the minister who sits at his “threshold” the Imam and his representative (his nâ’ib or his bâb, “threshold”).
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01731

There is no need to choose between these interpretations. What matters is precisely that they do not exclude one another. They—and others besides—are all possible because, even as they assign different functions to the characters, they preserve the identity of the same dramatic element. It is this: the Dator formarum, the Giver of Forms from whom our souls and our knowledge proceed, will keep the meeting arranged with the pilgrim before he set out.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01732

The pilgrim was sent into the earthly world for the very purpose of finding him there, and of finding him in the dazzling mirror that reflects the pilgrim’s own image. As for the meeting place, it perfectly illustrates the correspondence between spiritual perspectives—the same correspondence that enables Swedenborg to arrange the levels of his spiritual interpretation. The principle is this: what is above and at the origin, when it has come into our world and assumed a place in space, is found at the center, at the heart (see above, Book I, chapter IV, section 2).
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01733

The end of the mystical journey, in the tenth and final chapter of our treatise, reveals the ultimate secret. We must follow carefully the stages of this revelation, here expressed through the phenomenon of the mirror.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01734

First, at the city’s heart, the pilgrim discovers that the shaykh who governs it is himself: the shaykh is his own reflected image. The shock of this discovery awakens him to self-awareness. Once awake, he sees beside him the minister of his sovereign, faithful to their appointed meeting. Two details suggest that this minister is none other than Khezr: he stands beside the Spring of Life, and he invites the pilgrim to immerse himself in it.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01735

At the end of the “Tale of the Crimson Archangel,” we read that “if you are Khezr,” you too can pass through the defiles—the labyrinth—of Mount Qaf. And here, in our Indo-Persian tale, the pilgrim has indeed become Khezr so completely that he discovers the minister of his sovereign to be himself as well. The minister, too, is the reflection of the pilgrim’s own image.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01736

The pilgrim is then dazzled by a second encounter with the mirror. As before, the shock of that dazzling experience discloses a presence. This time it is his sovereign himself, also faithful to the appointed meeting, for the condition has now been fulfilled.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01737

But a momentous reversal is about to occur. Previously, the pilgrim had discovered that first the shaykh of his Personal City and then his sovereign’s wise minister were mirrors reflecting his own image. Now, at the final stage of his discovery, he realizes that he himself is the reflected image of his sovereign. He has become the mirror. His soul, his own self—the self known by the “I” that knows “itself” (recall our discussion above, chapter VI, sections 1 and 4)—is this sovereign, just as earlier it was the Gnostic’s personal angel. And he himself, the “I” that knows itself, is the sovereign’s reflected image.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01738

We can now understand why we recalled the initiate’s final discovery on emerging from Leonardo’s labyrinth into the eight-sided chamber of mirrors, which multiplies to infinity the image of the person standing at its center. In the end, the phenomenon of these mirrors is what enables us to understand the secret of the esoteric tawhîd, the innermost meaning of divine oneness.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01739

Here is the conclusion of our Indo-Persian initiation story: “When I had understood all these things, I discovered that the minister of my sovereign beside me was myself; the minister was my reflected image. I stood dazzled. And in that dazzling moment I met my sovereign himself. He ordered me to take a thread spun by a spider. He divided the thread in two, then joined it again into a single thread, saying to me: ‘The one multiplied by the one is the One (1 × 1 = 1).’ Then I understood his allusion: I discovered that my soul (nafsî, my ‘self’) is he himself, and that I am his reflected image.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01740

This symbol, 1 × 1 = 1, expresses something that is neither a vaguely mystical monism, in which everything loses its distinction, nor an abstract monotheism that isolates the personal divinity from the one to whom, and through whom, that divinity reveals itself as a person. Failure to understand this has led to many misinterpretations both of Sufi spiritual philosophy and of the experience to which it leads. The mystic first discovers images that reflect the image of his soul: the shaykh of the Personal City and the sovereign’s minister. Finally he discovers that he himself is the mirror reflecting his sovereign’s image.
